INFRAGUARD AI
Governance-by-Design for Bounded Incident Triage

72/72 STRUCTURE-VALID  •  29/72 EXACT SEVERITY

PROJECT DEFENCE
Adebodun Samuel Tomola  |  2025/A/MIT/0616
Supervisor: Dr. Emmanuel Mkpojiogu
Miva Open University  |  August 2026
textPreview: INFRAGUARD AI | Governance-by-Design for Bounded Incident Triage |  | 72/72 STRUCTURE-VALID  •  29/72 EXACT SEVERITY |  | PROJECT DEFENCE...

text:
[Timing] 0:00–0:20 (20 seconds)

Good afternoon. InfraGuard AI is a governance-by-design framework for bounded model-assisted incident triage. The result that frames this defence is simple: all 72 benchmark outputs passed the project's required verdict-structure and parser checks, but only 29 matched the expected severity. I will show what InfraGuard changes and why that gap makes its safeguards necessary.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Abstract and Sections 5.2, 5.4.2.2–5.4.2.3, 5.4.3 and 6.3
[/Sources]

name: Google Shape;89;g3ba14ccda94_0_28
text:
PROBLEM
• Logs, metrics and alerts remain fragmented
• Operators must correlate evidence, consult runbooks and judge severity
• Fluent model output can be well-formed yet unsafe

WHAT INFRAGUARD FIXES
A governed interpretation layer: bounded evidence, visible provenance and human-controlled action—not more monitoring or autonomous diagnosis.
textPreview: PROBLEM | • Logs, metrics and alerts remain fragmented | • Operators must correlate evidence, consult runbooks and judge severity | • Flu...

text:
[Timing] 0:20–1:05 (45 seconds)

Existing monitoring already detects symptoms, but it leaves operators to assemble the judgement. Evidence is spread across logs, metrics, alerts and runbooks, while severity and action still require human interpretation. Adding a language model alone does not solve that problem because a fluent answer can be inconsistent or confidently wrong. InfraGuard therefore does not replace monitoring. It adds a governed interpretation layer that bounds the evidence, records provenance, validates the verdict and keeps disruptive action under operator control.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Sections 1.1, 1.2–1.2.1, 2.4.5 and 6.2
[/Sources]

name: architecture-boundary
text: ACTION BOUNDARY  •  service/firewall changes require approval
textPreview: ACTION BOUNDARY  •  service/firewall changes require approval

text:
[Timing] 1:05–2:00 (55 seconds)

The workflow begins with selected telemetry from Loki, Prometheus, HTTP checks, Docker and CrowdSec. InfraGuard retrieves bounded runbook context from the local store, combines it with the telemetry and sends that evidence to the configured model. The response is forced into a structured verdict and validated before it reaches the operator. The operator reviews the verdict and decides what action, if any, to take. Notifications are allowed, but a CrowdSec ban requires explicit approval. Acknowledgement only masks qualifying rows in the default dashboard view; it does not stop inference, model calls or verdict storage.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Sections 3.3.2–3.3.6, 3.4.3–3.4.6 and 4.2.5–4.2.8
[/Sources]

text:
[Timing] 2:00–2:50 (50 seconds)

The primary contribution is the governance-by-design reference framework: bounded context, visible provenance, structured validation, operator approval and severity-aware visibility are designed into one incident-triage workflow. Its distinctive implemented construct is the fingerprint. It binds the condition signature to prompt version and model, so a changed reasoning context forces fresh review. Matching low-risk rows may be masked, but records and calls continue and high or critical findings remain visible. The claim is deliberately scoped: this combination is the contribution, while universal novelty is not claimed. Signature instability and same-model circularity remain limitations.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Sections 1.2.1, 2.2.4, 2.4.5, 3.4.5, 4.2.5, 5.3, 5.6.2 and 6.3

text:
[Timing] 2:50–3:30 (40 seconds)

The evaluation keeps unlike claims separate. Software verification used 148 automated tests and line coverage. Model behaviour used a frozen qwen2.5:3b benchmark: 24 fixtures repeated three times, producing 72 responses. Retrieval was checked separately with 12 labelled questions. The first human stream used two exploratory assessor-role reports. The separate SUS study used ten complete convenience-sample responses; they are not the same cohort or instrument. These streams do not constitute a live operational field evaluation or prove real-world diagnostic effectiveness.

[Sources]

text:
[Timing] 3:30–4:20 (50 seconds)

Controlled software verification was strong. The recorded 28 August run passed 148 tests with 87 percent statement coverage across 1,516 statements, and five reviewer-targeted modules reached 100 percent. For each of 12 labelled questions, at least one frozen relevant runbook appeared in the top four. The exploratory two-assessor means were higher with RAG in the frozen study. All 72 outputs passed required verdict-structure and parser checks; this was not a full JSON-Schema validation. The descriptive SUS mean was 79.25 from ten complete convenience-sample responses. These findings do not prove diagnostic or production effectiveness.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Sections 5.2–5.2.1, 5.4.2.2–5.4.2.3, 5.4.3 and 5.6.1; Appendices D–E

text:
[Timing] 4:20–5:20 (60 seconds)

For the tested qwen2.5:3b configuration, all 72 outputs passed the project's required verdict-structure and parser checks, but exact severity accuracy was only 40.3 percent—29 of 72—and macro-F1 was 0.383. Six gold-high responses were under-called as warning across two scenarios repeated three times. Only 10 of 24 scenarios produced one identical signature across all three repeats. These results show exactly where the artefact's value must be bounded. Parser checks protect expected form, not calibration. Human review, visible severity and controlled action are therefore mandatory design requirements.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Sections 5.4.2.2, 5.6.1–5.6.3 and 6.2–6.3; Tables 5.5–5.6; Appendix E
[/Sources]

name: Google Shape;89;g3ba14ccda94_0_28
text:
DEMONSTRATED IN THE EVALUATED ARTEFACT
• Bounded telemetry and runbook context
• Visible provenance and structured validation
• Operator approval before a CrowdSec ban
• Severity-aware fingerprinted acknowledgement

NOT DEMONSTRATED
Autonomous diagnosis; workload or alert-fatigue reduction; production effectiveness; population usability; cross-model/provider equivalence

NEXT EVIDENCE
Telemetry-derived signatures; comparative models; live field trials; larger panels; task-based usability
textPreview: DEMONSTRATED IN THE EVALUATED ARTEFACT | • Bounded telemetry and runbook context | • Visible provenance and structured validation | • Ope...

text:
[Timing] 5:20–6:00 (40 seconds)

InfraGuard demonstrates an inspectable, operator-controlled reference framework in the evaluated artefact. It combines telemetry and runbooks with visible provenance, structured validation, explicit approval before a CrowdSec ban and a fingerprinted acknowledgement mechanism that preserves high-severity visibility. The evaluation does not establish autonomous diagnosis, real-world workload or alert-fatigue reduction, production effectiveness, population usability or cross-model/provider equivalence. Next steps are telemetry-derived signatures, comparative models, live-workload field evaluation, larger independent panels and task-instrumented usability. InfraGuard's contribution is not autonomous diagnosis; it shows how model-assisted triage can be made inspectable, evidence-bounded and operator-controlled—and why those safeguards are necessary.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Sections 5.6.2–5.6.3 and 6.2–6.4
[/Sources]

text:
• Automation bias can produce misuse, disuse or complacency
• Trust should be calibrated to demonstrated reliability and visible evidence
• Alert fatigue makes repeated presentation—not inference—an operational concern
• Human-AI guidance requires capability disclosure, correction and user control
• Organisational AI governance requires accountable roles, controls and evidence
• Trustworthy AI turns principles into continuing risk and monitoring duties

Design implication — structured output never replaces operator judgement
textPreview: • Automation bias can produce misuse, disuse or complacency | • Trust should be calibrated to demonstrated reliability and visible eviden...

text:
Theoretical foundations are Design Science, organisational AI governance, trustworthy AI and appropriate reliance. Observability, SRE, AIOps and RAG are domain concepts; bounded context, provenance, validation, acknowledgement and approval are design constructs.
Alert fatigue is a motivation, not a measured outcome in this study.

[Sources]
- InfraGuard_AI_Masters_Project_REVISED_AFTER_28_AUGUST_REVIEW.docx, Sections 2.1.6 to 2.1.8 and 2.4.5
- Mäntymäki et al. (2022); Morley et al. (2020); NIST (2023, 2024); Raji et al. (2020); Lee and See (2004)
[/Sources]
